analysis.one_liner: Lets new TV providers skip local franchise negotiations to bring competition to single-provider cable markets.
analysis.headline: The bill died without any committee vote: referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on June 30, 2005, it saw no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, nearly all cable subscribers had only one wireline TV provider to choose from, and cable rates were rising faster than inflation. This bill would have let phone companies and other new entrants sell TV service without negotiating a separate franchise agreement in every town — instead paying local fees capped at the rates cable operators already pay. New providers would have kept some obligations (local public-access channels, must-carry rules, subscriber privacy, a ban on refusing service to lower-income areas) but would have been shielded from rate regulation by the FCC or states. The bill was introduced by Sen. Gordon Smith (R-OR) with Sen. John Rockefeller (D-WV) and died in committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers, most of whom had no wireline alternative: the bill's own findings said only 2% of cable subscribers had a choice of two or more wire-based video providers, and that rates were 15% lower where competition existed. New entrants — chiefly large telephone companies laying fiber — would also gain a faster path into the TV market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cable subscribers stuck with one provider

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits requiring a new video provider to obtain a local cable franchise where it already has the right to use public rights-of-way, removing a town-by-town negotiation barrier to entry [S2][S3].
Lets new providers pay local fees capped at the franchise-fee rates cable operators already pay, so local governments keep fee revenue [S2][S3].

Keeps real obligations on new entrants: retransmission-consent and must-carry rules, carriage of public-educational-government channels, subscriber-privacy protections, FCC consumer-service standards, and a ban on denying service to any group of residential subscribers because of the income of their area [S3].
The bill's findings cite GAO evidence that where wire-based video competition exists, cable rates are 15% lower, arguing competition would restrain rising cable prices [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators, who would face competitors for the first time in most markets. Local governments would lose the negotiating leverage they used under the franchise process to extract commitments like network build-outs and public-access facilities beyond basic channel carriage. And because the bill bars the FCC and states from regulating rates or terms for new providers, consumers in areas the new entrants choose not to build would keep paying monopoly prices with no regulatory backstop.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cable operators and local franchise authorities

drawbacks.text: The bill strips state and local authority over rates, terms, and conditions for new video providers, eliminating a regulatory backstop in areas where competition never arrives — entry would be voluntary, not universal [S2][S3].

It removes the local franchise process that communities used to negotiate benefits beyond fees, such as network build-out commitments and public-access facilities; the bill requires only that new providers carry PEG channels the local cable operator already carries [S3].
Competition would take years and reach only where it is profitable to build, so savings would be uneven across neighborhoods and regions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a genuine path to breaking up local cable monopolies, with real price effects where competition took hold, and it carried meaningful consumer protections including a ban on income-based redlining. But it paid for that competition with broad preemption of state and local oversight, and its benefits depended entirely on new entrants deciding to build — consumers in towns the phone companies passed over would have lost regulatory protection without gaining a competitor. A fair reading is that it traded local regulatory control for a chance at competition, and whether that trade was good depended on where you lived.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a markup or a floor vote before the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Gordon Smith (R-OR), joined by Sen. John Rockefeller (D-WV), introduced the Video Choice Act of 2005 on June 30, 2005 [S1][S3][S5].

The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation; the action history shows no committee markup, no vote, and no floor action for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, so the bill expired in committee [S1].
The bill's findings noted that only 2% of cable subscribers had a choice of two or more wire-based providers and that cable rates were rising faster than inflation [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent cable operators kept their markets without facing the federal shortcut for phone-company rivals, and local franchising authorities kept their negotiating leverage. Consumers waiting for a cable alternative got nothing from this Congress.

for.name: Sen. Gordon Smith (R-OR)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. John Rockefeller IV (D-WV)
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction; it was introduced 'for himself and Mr. Rockefeller.'

for.name: Large telephone companies
for.what_they_did: Were widely reported to be pressing Congress and state legislatures in this period for relief from town-by-town cable franchise requirements so they could enter the TV market with their new fiber networks.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill: no markup, no report, no vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican with the top Democrat as original co-sponsor and drew cosponsors of both parties, but with no roll call it is unknown how the chamber would have divided.

industries.note: Incumbent cable operators would have faced new competitors in markets where they were effectively the only choice, and their local franchise arrangements would no longer have been a barrier to entry. Their interest in preserving the status quo ran against subscribers paying above-inflation rate increases.

Phone companies laying fiber would have gained a fast, uniform path into the video market without negotiating franchises city by city, largely shielded from rate and terms regulation. Their market entry is what would have delivered the price competition to consumers, though only where they chose to build.

Local governments would have kept fee revenue, capped at cable rates, but lost the franchise process they used to negotiate build-outs and public-access facilities. Some of what they negotiated served residents directly; some served municipal coffers and control.
